title: Strat Chat – Responsive Teaching
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien continues his Strat Chat series on checking for understanding by asking the harder question of what a teacher does once the data comes back. He argues that a check is meaningless unless it informs the next instructional move, and defends the term responsive teaching against the charge that it is simply what great teachers already do, since curriculum pressure leads many to respond too late. He sets out practical thresholds: roughly 80 percent success means move on, 50 to 80 percent calls for modest tier 2 fixes such as cold calling or sentence stems, and below 50 percent demands careful diagnosis of knowledge, application or misconception problems. He adds that newer teachers should be honest with students when a lesson needs revisiting. The closing move is a caution that a successful re-check is still only performance, illustrated by his Year 12 Economics class, so spacing and interleaving must follow the response.
points: A check for understanding is tokenistic unless the result changes what the teacher does next, so the response is the point of the check.

Shaun Brien offers a simple threshold model: above about 80 percent success move on, 50 to 80 percent calls for light tier 2 intervention, and below 50 percent signals a flaw in the instruction itself.
Below 50 percent, diagnose whether students lack the knowledge, cannot apply it, or hold a misconception, then use worked examples with think alouds or re-teach in different words.
Newer teachers should feel free to park a topic and say openly that it will be revisited, which beats ploughing forward without understanding.
Even a perfect response only yields performance, so spaced practice and interleaving are needed before anyone can claim learning, as his Year 12 income effect example shows.
quotes: Responsive teaching refers to the actions we take after the data we gain from a check for understanding. It is all about how we use that data to meaningfully inform our next steps to ensure the majority of our students are showing their understanding successfully.

Generally, we assume that our tier 1 instruction will effectively land for around 80% of our students. If the number is above that? Brilliant, you nailed it, move on to your next point (assuming the check was pitched at the correct level of difficulty and didn’t provide a false positive).

The next possibility is that somewhere between 50 to 80% of the class is showing understanding. In this case some level of tier 2 intervention is definitely required, but it may not need to be too in-depth or intense. This can often be resolved by cold calling multiple students to explain their answers and then having one of the incorrect students explain why that answer is correct. This could also be resolved by simply having another check for understanding after you explain the answer or providing more scaffolding for a similar question such as sentence stems.

Finally, in the worst case scenario you may have less than 50% of students show understanding. This shows that there’s been a flaw in your instruction despite your best intentions. Maybe the sidetracked story about your glory days was slightly too detached from the key knowledge and left the students confused, or you hadn’t modeled thinking and the types of questions students will need to respond to enough.

This all sounds simple and if you’ve been teaching a subject for many years it will be. If you’re newer to teaching or a subject this will sometimes require parking the topic and telling the students you’re going to prepare for it again as it hasn’t quite gone to plan. There’s nothing wrong with being open with the students about this and bringing them on the journey with you. You can spend the first part of your next lesson tackling it again from another angle and that is far superior to just ploughing forward with no understanding from anyone.

Well no, this is still just performance and not learning. It isn’t until these students can consistently pull this information from their long term memory in future lessons that we can truly say that learning has happened. This is why it is integral that even if we are perfectly responsive in our lessons that we space practice over time and interleave content throughout the rest of the teaching year.
